stages.title: How the Web Works & Semantic HTML
stages.description: What really happens between typing a URL and seeing a page, and how to write HTML that means something to browsers, search engines and assistive technology.
learningObjectives: How a browser loads and renders a page

explainBack.question: What happens between typing a URL and seeing the page, and why does semantic HTML matter for that page?
rubric: States that the domain name is resolved to an IP address (DNS)
Explains that the browser sends an HTTP request and receives HTML in the response
Explains that the browser parses the HTML and loads linked CSS and JavaScript before rendering
Explains that semantic elements convey meaning to assistive technology and search engines, not just appearance
Gives a concrete semantic-vs-generic example (e.g. <nav> vs <div>, <button> vs clickable <div>)

resources.title: What happens when you type a URL into your browser?
resources.description: A short visual walkthrough of the full journey from typing a URL to seeing the rendered page.
keyPoints: Follows a URL from the address bar to a rendered page
Covers the DNS lookup that finds the server's IP address
Covers the connection and HTTP request/response exchange
Covers how the browser turns the response into a page

resources.title: How the web works
resources.description: MDN's beginner explanation of clients, servers, DNS, TCP/IP, packets and HTTP.
keyPoints: Browsers (clients) request pages and servers send back the files
DNS translates a domain name into the server's IP address
TCP/IP moves data across the internet in packets
HTTP is the request/response language; status codes like 200 and 404 report results

resources.title: Populating the page: how browsers work
resources.description: How a browser turns an HTML response into pixels: parsing, the DOM and CSSOM, and the render pipeline.
keyPoints: DNS lookup, TCP and TLS happen before the first request
HTML is parsed into the DOM while a preload scanner fetches CSS, JS and images
CSS is parsed into the CSSOM
DOM and CSSOM combine into a render tree, then layout, paint and compositing

resources.title: Structuring documents
resources.description: How to structure a page with semantic sectioning elements and why that matters.
keyPoints: header, nav, main, article, section, aside and footer describe what each part of a page is
Assistive technology uses these elements to let people jump between regions
div and span are for when no semantic element fits
Use main once per page for the unique content

resources.title: HTML: A good basis for accessibility
resources.description: Why correct HTML elements give you keyboard and screen-reader support for free, including accessible forms.
keyPoints: A real <button> is keyboard and screen-reader accessible; a clickable <div> is not
Associate each form control with a <label> using the for attribute
Headings, alt text and table headers help screen-reader users
Don't remove native keyboard behaviour that semantic elements provide

stages.title: CSS Layout & Responsive Design
stages.description: How the box model sizes elements, how the cascade decides which styles win, and how Flexbox and Grid build layouts that adapt to any screen.

explainBack.question: When would you choose Flexbox over Grid, and how does the box model affect an element's size?
rubric: Explains Flexbox as one-dimensional (a row or a column) and Grid as two-dimensional (rows and columns)
Names the box model layers: content, padding, border, margin
Explains that box-sizing: border-box includes padding and border in the declared width
Explains making layouts responsive with media queries or intrinsic, flexible sizing

resources.title: Flexbox or grid - How to decide?
resources.description: A CSS specialist's practical approach to choosing between Flexbox and Grid for a given layout.
keyPoints: Compares when Flexbox or Grid suits a layout
Flexbox lets content size itself along one axis
Grid defines rows and columns up front
Choose based on the layout you need, not habit

resources.title: The box model
resources.description: Content, padding, border and margin, the standard vs alternative box model, and margin collapsing.
keyPoints: Every element is a box: content, padding, border, margin
By default width sets only the content area, so padding and border add to it
box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border
Block and inline elements treat the box model differently

resources.title: Learn CSS
resources.description: A free, evergreen CSS course covering the box model, cascade, specificity, Flexbox and Grid.
keyPoints: Everything CSS displays is a box
The cascade and specificity decide which rule wins
Flexbox lays out items in one dimension
Grid lays out rows and columns in two dimensions

resources.title: Responsive web design
resources.description: Media queries, flexible layouts, responsive images and typography, and the viewport meta tag.
keyPoints: Responsive design is an approach, not a single technology
Media queries apply CSS at specific viewport sizes, often mobile-first
Flexbox and Grid are responsive by default with flexible units
The viewport meta tag is required for mobile layouts

stages.title: JavaScript Fundamentals
stages.description: The core language: values and types, functions, scope, arrays and objects, and responding to events in the page.

explainBack.question: Explain the difference between let, const and var, and what a closure is.
rubric: Explains that let and const are block-scoped while var is function-scoped
Explains that const prevents reassignment but not mutation of objects
Defines a closure as a function that keeps access to variables from its outer scope after that scope has finished
Gives a practical closure example (e.g. a counter or a function factory)

resources.title: Learn Closures In 7 Minutes
resources.description: A short, example-driven explanation of closures.
keyPoints: A closure lets a function use variables from where it was created
Inner functions keep access to outer variables after the outer function returns
Walks through practical closure examples

resources.title: Variable scope, closure
resources.description: Block scope, lexical environments and how every JavaScript function closes over its surroundings.
keyPoints: let and const are confined to the block they're declared in
Every function remembers the lexical environment it was created in
That's why inner functions can use outer variables later
Environments stay in memory while a function still references them

resources.title: The old "var"
resources.description: How var differs from let and const: function scope, hoisting and redeclaration.
keyPoints: var ignores blocks and is scoped to the whole function
var declarations are hoisted to the top of the function
var can be redeclared; let cannot
Old code used IIFEs to fake block scope

resources.title: const
resources.description: Reference for const: block-scoped, cannot be reassigned, but objects it points to can still change.
keyPoints: const creates a block-scoped binding
A const binding can't be reassigned
Properties of a const object can still be added, changed or removed
const makes the binding constant, not the value

resources.title: The Modern JavaScript Tutorial
resources.description: A free, complete JavaScript tutorial from fundamentals through objects, data types, functions and browser events.
keyPoints: Part 1 covers fundamentals, objects, data types and functions
Arrays and objects are covered in dedicated chapters
Part 2 covers the DOM and browser events
Free and open-source

stages.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
stages.description: Why JavaScript doesn't wait, how the event loop works, and how promises, async/await and fetch let you work with data that arrives later.

explainBack.question: Why doesn't fetch return data immediately, and how do async/await make it easier to handle?
rubric: Explains that network work is asynchronous and non-blocking
States that fetch returns a Promise
Explains that await pauses the async function until the Promise settles without blocking the main thread
Explains error handling with try/catch AND checking response.ok, because fetch does not reject on HTTP error statuses

resources.title: What the heck is the event loop anyway? | Philip Roberts | JSConf EU
resources.description: The classic conference talk that visualises the call stack, browser APIs, the callback queue and the event loop.
keyPoints: JavaScript runs one thing at a time on a single call stack
Slow work is handed to browser APIs so the stack stays free
Finished callbacks wait in a queue until the stack is empty
Blocking the stack freezes the page

resources.title: Promise
resources.description: What a promise is, its states, and how then, catch and finally handle results.
keyPoints: A promise starts pending and settles once, as fulfilled or rejected
then() attaches handlers for success and failure
catch() handles errors; finally() runs cleanup either way

resources.title: Async/await
resources.description: How async functions and await make promise-based code read top to bottom, including error handling.
keyPoints: async functions always return a promise
await pauses the function until the promise settles, without blocking the engine
A rejected promise makes await throw, so use try/catch
Top-level await only works in modules

resources.title: Using the Fetch API
resources.description: How to make requests with fetch, read responses, and handle both network and HTTP errors.
keyPoints: fetch returns a Promise that resolves to a Response
fetch does not reject on HTTP errors like 404, so check response.ok
Wrap calls in try/catch to handle network failures
Reading the body (json(), text()) is also asynchronous

resources.title: The Async Await Episode I Promised
resources.description: A fast, code-heavy tour of promises and async/await, including common mistakes.
keyPoints: Shows how promises chain
Rewrites promise chains with async/await
Covers error handling and running promises concurrently

stages.title: TypeScript Essentials
stages.description: Why typed JavaScript catches bugs before they run, and the everyday types, unions, narrowing and generics you'll use constantly.

explainBack.question: What problem does TypeScript solve, and how does narrowing work on a union type?
rubric: Explains that static type checking catches type errors before the code runs
Explains that types are erased at compile time and don't exist at runtime
Explains that a union type means a value can be one of several types
Explains narrowing (typeof, in, or a discriminant property) letting TypeScript know the specific type inside a branch

resources.title: TypeScript Tutorial for Beginners
resources.description: A beginner-friendly video course introducing TypeScript's type system and tooling.
keyPoints: Why TypeScript exists and how it compiles to JavaScript
Basic types, arrays, tuples and objects
Type aliases, unions and optional values

resources.title: The Basics
resources.description: The official handbook's introduction to static type checking, and how types are erased when compiling.
keyPoints: TypeScript catches errors like calling a non-function before the code runs
It flags typos and missing properties
Type annotations are removed when compiling to JavaScript
Strictness can be tuned for gradual adoption

resources.title: Everyday Types
resources.description: The types you'll use daily: primitives, objects, unions, type aliases and interfaces.
keyPoints: Primitive types mirror JavaScript's typeof results
Object types can have optional properties
Union types combine several possible types with |
Type aliases and interfaces both describe shapes; interfaces can be extended by merging

resources.title: Narrowing
resources.description: How TypeScript narrows a union to a specific type using control flow checks.
keyPoints: typeof checks narrow primitive unions
The in operator narrows by property presence
Discriminated unions narrow using a shared literal property
TypeScript tracks narrowing through control flow

resources.title: Generics
resources.description: Writing reusable functions and types with type parameters instead of any.
keyPoints: Type parameters keep type information instead of falling back to any
extends constrains what a generic type must have
Interfaces and classes can be generic too

stages.title: React Fundamentals
stages.description: Building UIs from components: JSX, props, rendering lists with keys, conditional rendering, and how data flows down the tree.

explainBack.question: What are props, and why does React need a key when rendering a list?
rubric: Explains props as read-only inputs passed from a parent component to a child
Explains that data flows down the component tree
Explains that keys give list items a stable identity across renders
Explains why using the array index as a key breaks when items are reordered or inserted

resources.title: React JS 19 Full Course 2025 | Build an App and Master React in 2 Hours
resources.description: A project-based React 19 course that builds an app while introducing components, props, state and hooks.
keyPoints: Components and JSX in React 19
Passing data with props
Rendering lists and conditional UI
Builds a complete app along the way

resources.title: Describing the UI
resources.description: The official chapter covering components, JSX, props, conditional rendering, lists and purity.
keyPoints: Components are functions that return markup
JSX rules and embedding JavaScript with curly braces
Conditional rendering with if, && and ternaries
Rendering lists with map() and keys

resources.title: Passing Props to a Component
resources.description: How parents pass data to children with props, and why props are read-only.
keyPoints: Parents pass information to children through props
Props are immutable snapshots; each render gets new props

Use state, not props, for interactivity

resources.title: Rendering Lists
resources.description: Rendering arrays with map and filter, and why every list item needs a stable key.
keyPoints: Keys let React match list items between renders

resources.title: Tutorial: Tic-Tac-Toe

keyPoints: Build reusable components that pass data through props

stages.title: Hooks & State
stages.description: Making components remember things with useState, syncing with the outside world with useEffect, and knowing when you don't need an effect at all.

explainBack.question: Why does useEffect need a dependency array?
rubric: Explains that effects run after render
Explains that the array lists the values the effect depends on, and the effect re-runs when one of them changes
Explains that an empty array means the effect runs after mount only, with cleanup on unmount
Explains that missing dependencies cause stale values
Explains the purpose of the cleanup function

resources.title: Learn useEffect In 13 Minutes
resources.description: A focused explanation of useEffect, its dependency array and cleanup.
keyPoints: Effects run after the component renders
The dependency array controls when the effect re-runs
An empty array runs the effect once after mount
Return a cleanup function to undo the effect

resources.title: State: A Component's Memory
resources.description: Why regular variables don't survive re-renders and how useState gives components memory.
keyPoints: State persists between renders; local variables don't
useState returns the value and a setter that triggers a re-render

resources.title: Synchronizing with Effects
resources.description: What effects are for, when they run, how dependencies control re-running, and why cleanup matters.
keyPoints: Effects run after rendering, to sync with systems outside React
React skips an effect when its dependencies haven't changed
An empty array runs the effect once when the component appears
Cleanup runs before the next effect and on unmount

resources.title: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects
resources.description: Why every reactive value an effect reads must be a dependency, and the bugs you get when one is missing.
keyPoints: Props, state and component variables are reactive
Every reactive value an effect uses must be a dependency
Missing dependencies leave the effect using stale values

resources.title: Sharing State Between Components
resources.description: Lifting state up to the closest common parent so components stay in sync.
keyPoints: Move shared state to the closest common parent
Pass the value down as props
Pass event handlers down so children can request changes

resources.title: You Might Not Need an Effect
resources.description: When to compute values during render instead of storing them in state or syncing them with an effect.
keyPoints: Calculate values from props and state during render instead of storing them
Redundant state gets out of sync and causes bugs
Use useMemo only for expensive calculations

stages.title: Next.js App Router & Rendering
stages.description: File-based routing, layouts, Server and Client Components, and how Next.js decides whether a route renders statically or per request.

explainBack.question: What is the difference between a Server Component and a Client Component, and when does a route render statically versus dynamically?
rubric: Explains that Server Components render on the server and ship no component JavaScript to the browser
Explains that Client Components ('use client') are needed for state, effects and event handlers, and are hydrated in the browser
Explains that a route renders statically when it uses no request-time data
Explains that a route renders dynamically when it uses request data such as cookies, headers or searchParams

resources.title: Next.js 15 Tutorial - 52 - Server and Client Components
resources.description: A focused lesson from a well-known Next.js series on when to use Server vs Client Components.

resources.title: Layouts and Pages
resources.description: File-system routing in the App Router: pages, layouts, nested routes and dynamic segments. (Docs v16.3.7)
keyPoints: Folders define route segments; page files make them public

resources.title: Server and Client Components
resources.description: When to use Server vs Client Components, how they render, and how hydration works. (Docs v16.3.7)

resources.title: Static and Dynamic Rendering

resources.title: Error Handling
resources.description: Expected errors, error.js boundaries, notFound(), and global-error. (Docs v16.3.6)

resources.title: App Router: Next.js Foundations course

keyPoints: Routing with nested layouts and pages

stages.title: Data Mutations & Server Actions

explainBack.question: How does a Server Action handle a form submission, and why must you still validate input on the server?

resources.title: Next.js 15 Tutorial - 74 - Forms with Server Actions

resources.title: How to create forms with Server Actions

resources.title: 'use server' directive

keyPoints: Create, update and delete records with Server Actions

stages.title: Databases & Prisma

stages.title: Authentication & Sessions
